video_title: Randy Cohen, Professor of Entrepreneurship & Finance Harvard Business School Co-Founder PEO Partners
gist: HBS professor Randy Cohen (co-founder, PEO Partners) argues LBOs are structurally forced to buy companies matching all five Fama-French factors (high profitability, high payout, low multiple, low risk, small size), so a public portfolio of ~200 matched stocks with ~0.3-0.4x extra leverage and a put-spread-style hedge can replicate PE returns while charging ~100bp versus PE's 700+bp, enabling a 60/40 to 50/30/20 shift. He also covers market puzzles (momentum's -120% 2009 crash, ticker-confusion anomalies like CUBA and MCI), new inefficient markets as the source of durable alpha, and LLMs like Claude transforming finance research.

insights.claim: Cohen argues an LBO is economically forced to target companies with high profitability, high payout, low multiple, low risk and small size — exactly the five Fama-French factors — because paying 9–12% interest on roughly two-thirds debt means servicing 6–8% of enterprise value in cash annually.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: PE returns can be largely explained, and replicated, with public-market factor exposures.

insights.claim: Cohen says typical LBO debt has fallen from about three-quarters to about two-thirds of capital and borrowing costs have risen from roughly 7–8% to 9–12% as interest rates rose.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Higher financing costs further narrow LBO targets to cheap, cash-generative firms.

insights.claim: A company bought at 30x earnings yields only 3.3% versus the 6–8% of EV needed for interest, so LBO-able targets must trade at low multiples, and high-growth reinvesters like Amazon are unsuitable because interest payments would starve growth.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Explains PE's structural value tilt.

insights.claim: Cohen estimates the appropriate incremental leverage to replicate LBOs in public markets is only about 0.3–0.4 turns (LBO-able public companies run ~40–50% debt vs ~60–70% in LBO deals), a figure CPPIB's Don Raymond suggested 26 years ago and Cohen now agrees with; it adds about 2–3% a year.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Liquid PE needs modest, not 2:1, leverage.

insights.claim: Cohen says liquid PE should lag traditional PE by about 3–6% a year gross (no inside information, no operational improvements net of control premium, hedge costs), but because PE charges over 700bp a year in fees per a CalPERS study versus ~100bp for a liquid vehicle, it can match or beat PE net.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Fee gap is the core economic case for PE replication products.
insights.quote: PE, according to CalPERS study, charges over 700 basis points a year in fees

insights.claim: Cohen positions liquid PE not as a PE replacement but as a way for investors below million-dollar minimums to move from 60/40 to 50/30/20, and as a liquidity buffer or completion portfolio for institutions already in PE.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Target market is retail/wealth channels plus institutional liquidity management.
insights.quote: this is a solution to take their portfolio from 60/40 to 50/30/20

insights.claim: Because PE reports smoothed marks (Cliff Asness's 'volatility laundering'), a levered public replica that falls 25–30% when PE claims -10% would enrage investors, so liquid PE must overlay a hedge such as a 95–85 put spread or something smarter, without overspending on insurance.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Hedge design and cost are central to liquid PE's viability.

insights.claim: Cohen describes the construction: find ~200 public companies maximally similar to the ~10,000 positions held by ~1,000 U.S. LBO funds, filtering out matched names already at high multiples or unprofitable, then buy e.g. $1.3B of stock per $1B of capital and hedge.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Concrete replication recipe: industry match + factor screen + 1.3x leverage + hedge.

insights.claim: Cohen says accurate replication requires PE holdings data, which is only partially available commercially at high cost; full visibility requires partnering with one of a handful of firms that see the entire PE universe.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Proprietary holdings data is a competitive moat in PE replication.

insights.claim: Cohen says liquid PE does not track PE quarter by quarter because PE managers 'get to decide what the numbers are', but historically it has delivered comparable downside volatility and post-fee average returns to average (not top-quartile) PE since his 2000 HBS speech.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Judge replication on long-run risk/return, not quarterly tracking.

insights.claim: PE has become heavily weighted in software and services after recognizing early that software shifted from vaporware to steady profits; early-2000s PE was underweight software and focused on brownfield industrials.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: PE replication portfolios now carry significant software exposure amid 'SaaS apocalypse' uncertainty.

insights.claim: In public markets healthcare is less than twice as big as banking, but in PE/LBO there is about 15 times as much healthcare as banking, implying large sector over/underweights in a PE-replicating portfolio.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Liquid PE is a large healthcare overweight vs the S&P.

insights.claim: Cohen and Christopher Polk found that buying the lowest-multiple stocks within each sector, rather than the lowest-multiple stocks overall, produced a far better-diversified value portfolio with much lower volatility and slightly higher average returns.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Sector-neutral value construction dominates naive value screens.

insights.claim: Cohen says around 2013 the 10 biggest companies were about 17% of the market, whereas now about seven companies are roughly 30%, more than doubling concentration.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Index investors carry unprecedented single-theme risk.

insights.claim: Cohen notes 2013's top companies (JPMorgan Chase, Exxon Mobil, Johnson & Johnson, Microsoft) were tightly tied to the broad economy, while today's leaders cluster in software/high-tech including Tesla and Nvidia, decoupling index leadership from the economy.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Diversifying sleeves with different return drivers matter more now.

insights.claim: Dean Curnutt argues investors should not fight the Magnificent 7 but need a sleeve with different underlying businesses and return drivers, which liquid PE can provide.
insights.speaker: Dean Curnutt
insights.so_what: Positions liquid PE as a concentration hedge.

insights.claim: Cohen's dissertation found, contrary to his agency hypothesis, that individual investors rather than institutions sell too much at market bottoms, with institutions buying from them — deepening the puzzle of high expected returns after crashes.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Retail capitulation, not institutional career risk, drives bottoms.

insights.claim: In Cohen's AQR momentum case, long-top-decile/short-bottom-decile momentum earned about 15% a year over 80 years, then lost about 120% in 2009 as crushed financials like Citigroup (from ~99 cents to ~$4) snapped back.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Momentum crashes occur in sharp junk rallies after crises.

insights.claim: Cohen shows the 81-year arithmetic average of momentum is still about 13.5% including 2009, but a buy-and-hold allocation would have been wiped out while an annually rebalanced 10-strategy portfolio would only lose 12% that year — a lesson in geometric vs arithmetic returns.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Rebalancing and position sizing determine whether high-return factors are survivable.

insights.claim: Cohen says the evidence for momentum as overreaction was slightly stronger than underreaction when he last checked, though he and Curnutt are intuitively drawn to the near-rational underreaction story.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Mechanism for momentum remains contested.

insights.claim: Cohen cites name-confusion anomalies: Orange County, California's derivatives debacle hit unrelated Orange County munis; ticker MCI fell on news for MCIC; and closed-end fund CUBA rose over 100% for weeks when Obama opened relations with Cuba despite no Cuba link.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Obvious mispricings exist but are hard to arbitrage due to borrow and squeeze risk.
insights.quote: these things are not as easy to take advantage of as as you might like

insights.claim: Mark Mitchell's study of 3Com/Palm-style negative stub trades, executed with his own money, revealed hidden risks such as the parent buying out the subsidiary above market, causing losses on both legs.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: 'Locked-in' arbitrages carry corporate-action and borrow risks.

insights.claim: Cohen argues active management will not die because new markets keep appearing — Chinese stocks with short-sale limits, newly investable markets like Pakistan, new derivatives, crypto and prediction markets — and each starts inefficient before maturing.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Hunt for alpha in nascent markets rather than mature U.S. large caps.
insights.quote: anything new that comes along starts off as a very inefficient market

insights.claim: Cohen says convertible arbitrage offered fairly easy money in the 1990s but now requires intense work to extract alpha, illustrating the inefficient-to-efficient lifecycle.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Strategy returns decay as capital arrives.

insights.claim: Cohen says negative nominal rates showed intuition can fail: shorting negative-yielding bonds seemed obvious but yields often went much more negative than people thought possible.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Apparent floors in rates are not reliable.

insights.claim: Lauren Cohen's pre-generative-AI research found that firms whose 10-K risk-factor sections changed in any direction from the prior year subsequently saw their stocks perform badly on average, because lawyers avoid changes unless something scary is coming.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Text changes in filings are a tradable negative signal.
insights.quote: There was any change in the risk statement in any direction

insights.claim: Cohen says tools like Claude make previously RA-intensive research ideas trivially easy, and a scholar now at a top quant fund uses Claude instead of asking staff to crunch numbers all weekend; screening 50 ideas to find six worth verifying is 'game-changing'.
insights.speaker: Randy Cohen
insights.so_what: Quant funds are internalizing AI-driven signal discovery; published anomaly alpha may decay faster.
